facts.fact_text: The case concerns a protest against a preannounced eviction of a squatted building.
The applicants argue that they had no violent intentions.
On 1 July 2011 a message on the website of Independent Media Centre (www.indymedia.nl) called on sympathisers to gather outside the Schijnheilig squat on 5 July 2011.

The message on www.indymedia.nl called on sympathisers to gather outside the Schijnheilig squat on 5 July 2011 "to make a spectacular statement protesting against an empty city and call for 'free space', for places where creativity and not money rules".
On 2 July 2011 a call for protest in the form of "poetry, singing, dancing, screaming, jumping [or] sending an angry letter" appeared on another website.
On 5 July 2011, at around 6 a.m., some 150 people gathered in front of and around the Schijnheilig squat at Passeerdersgracht in Amsterdam.

During the gathering on 5 July 2011 the participants danced, played instruments, stood close and talked to each other, and chanted slogans such as "Squatting's here to stay" and "You Government puppets".
Most of the participants in the gathering on 5 July 2011 were recognisable and wore plain clothes.
Some of the participants in the gathering on 5 July 2011 were dressed up in costumes or wedding dresses.

The limited jurisdiction judge was of the opinion that the gathering of the group of persons on 5 July 2011 was initially characterised more as a demonstration as referred to in the Public Assemblies Act than an unlawful gathering entailing disorder in the sense of section 2.2 of the Amsterdam general municipal by-law (APV).
The limited jurisdiction judge concluded that at the outset of the gathering on 5 July 2011 there was a demonstration within the meaning of the Public Assemblies Act (Wet openbare manifestaties).

In their appeals on points of law to the Supreme Court, the applicants submitted that the Amsterdam Court of Appeal had failed to recognise that the protest had been a "peaceful assembly" within the meaning of Article 11 of the Convention.
The Advocate General noted that freedom of assembly must be regarded as one of the foundations of a democratic society and may not be interpreted restrictively according to the Court.
The Advocate General noted that the scope of Article 11 of the Convention includes all kinds of gatherings, including demonstrations and blockades.
The Advocate General noted that the mere circumstance that there is a risk of disturbances during a demonstration does not mean that the protection of Article 11 of the Convention will lapse.

The Advocate General noted that the protection of Article 11 of the Convention does not lapse if some participants in the demonstration have violent intentions or if marginal or sporadic violent or other criminal behaviour is displayed.

The Advocate General noted that according to settled case-law of the Court, the notion of 'peaceful assembly' does not include 'a demonstration where the organizers and participants have violent intentions which result in public disorder'.

Section B, paragraph 86 of the OSCE/ODIHR Guidelines on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly (3rd edition) provides that all assemblies shall be presumed to be peaceful in the absence of convincing evidence that the organisers and/or a significant number of participants intend to use, advocate or incite imminent violence.

Section B, paragraph 87 of the OSCE/ODIHR Guidelines on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly (3rd edition) provides that law enforcement officials must differentiate between peaceful and non-peaceful participants since only those who themselves take part in violence forfeit the legal guarantee of their right to assemble.

Section B, paragraph 87 of the OSCE/ODIHR Guidelines on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly (3rd edition) provides that state intervention should target individual wrongdoers, rather than all participants more generally, unless that is impossible due to the massive nature of the violence committed.

General Comment No. 37 on the right of peaceful assembly (Article 21) of the Human Rights Committee, adopted at its 129th session (29 June–24 July 2020, UN Doc. CCPR/C/GC/37), provides that the use of disguises should not in itself be deemed to signify violent intent (at point 60).
The applicants argue that their arrest amounted to an unjustified interference with their right to freedom of peaceful assembly.
The applicants argue that their prosecution amounted to an unjustified interference with their right to freedom of peaceful assembly.
The applicants argue that their conviction amounted to an unjustified interference with their right to freedom of peaceful assembly.
At 6.57 a.m. on 5 July 2011 the Police Commissioner ordered those present in front of the Schijnheilig squat to disperse and leave Passeerdersgracht in the direction of an adjacent street.
After issuing two additional orders to disperse, the Police Commissioner instructed the Mobile Unit (Mobiele Eenheid, a special operations unit of the police) to carry out a charge.
Using protective shields and wielding truncheons, the Mobile Unit advanced and cleared the area in front of the Schijnheilig squat.
At 8.37 a.m. on 5 July 2011 the Police Commissioner informed the participants that they were all under arrest.

A total of 138 persons, including the applicants, were arrested on 5 July 2011 on suspicion of participating in an unlawful gathering or otherwise disturbing public order, prohibited and made punishable by the Amsterdam general municipal by-law (Algemene Plaatselijke Verordening; the APV).
The 138 arrested persons, including the applicants, were arraigned before the assistant public prosecutor on 5 July 2011.

On an unspecified date, the applicants were summonsed to appear before the limited jurisdiction judge (kantonrechter) of the Amsterdam Regional Court on suspicion of participating in an unlawful gathering or otherwise disturbing public order, contrary to section 2.2(1) of the Amsterdam general municipal by-law (APV).

On an unspecified date, the applicants were summonsed to appear before the limited jurisdiction judge (kantonrechter) of the Amsterdam Regional Court on suspicion of failing to comply with a police order to disperse, contrary to section 2.2(3) of the Amsterdam general municipal by-law (APV).

By separate judgments of 14 June 2013 the limited jurisdiction judge (kantonrechter) of the Amsterdam Regional Court found proven that the applicants had failed to comply with police orders to disperse.

The Amsterdam Court of Appeal found it proven that the applicants had participated in an unlawful gathering or otherwise disturbed public order in breach of section 2.2(1) of the Amsterdam general municipal by-law (APV).
The Amsterdam Court of Appeal found it proven that the applicants had failed to comply with a police order to disperse in breach of section 2.2(3) of the Amsterdam general municipal by-law (APV).
The Amsterdam Court of Appeal sentenced each applicant to two fines of 50 euros (EUR), each fine to be replaced by one day's detention in the event of non-payment.
By separate judgments of 11 April 2017 the Supreme Court (Hoge Raad) dismissed the applicants' appeals on points of law.
By its judgments of 11 April 2017 the Supreme Court upheld the judgments of the Amsterdam Court of Appeal.

Section 2.2(1) of the Amsterdam general municipal by-law (APV) of 2008 prohibits, on or near the public road or in a building or vessel accessible to the public, participating in an unlawful gathering (samenscholing), defined in section 2.1(4) as 'a gathering of people who assume a threatening attitude, have malicious intentions or appear threatening', or, either as a member of a group or individually, imposing oneself unnecessarily, harassing others, fighting or otherwise disturbing public order (de orde verstoren).

Section 2.2(3) of the Amsterdam general municipal by-law (APV) of 2008 requires a person who is present on or near the public road at an event that attracts members of the public or at any occurrence that causes or is likely to cause disturbances (ongeregeldheden), or who is moving towards that event or occurrence, to immediately obey an order given by a police officer to move away in a given direction.

Section 2.2(4) of the Amsterdam general municipal by-law (APV) of 2008 provides that the prohibitions in section 2.2 do not apply to demonstrations and assemblies within the meaning of the Public Assemblies Act.
The Amsterdam general municipal by-law (APV) of 2008 was laid down by the local council (gemeenteraad).

An explanatory note to section 2.2 of the Amsterdam general municipal by-law (APV) provides that regulation of demonstrations does not fall within the competence of the municipal legislature and that gatherings to which the Public Assemblies Act applies are excluded by section 2.2(4) of the APV.

The explanatory note to section 2.2 of the Amsterdam general municipal by-law (APV) provides that the Mayor must base any measures regarding demonstrations on the Public Assemblies Act, which grants the Mayor powers to take measures in the event of disturbances and contains penal provisions in this regard.
A breach of section 2.2(1) of the Amsterdam general municipal by-law (APV) is a minor offence under section 154 of the Municipality Act.
A breach of section 2.2(3) of the Amsterdam general municipal by-law (APV) is a minor offence under section 154 of the Municipality Act.

A breach of section 2.2(1) or section 2.2(3) of the Amsterdam general municipal by-law (APV) is punishable by a term of imprisonment not exceeding three months or a second-category fine under section 6.1 of the APV.

Article 9(1) of the Constitution of the Kingdom of the Netherlands (Grondwet) provides that the right of assembly (vergadering) and demonstration (betoging) shall be recognised, without prejudice to the responsibility of everyone under the law.

Article 9(2) of the Constitution of the Kingdom of the Netherlands provides that rules to protect health, in the interest of traffic, and to combat or prevent disorder may be laid down by Act of Parliament.

The Public Assemblies Act (Wet openbare manifestaties) is an act laid down by Parliament that regulates the exercise of and restrictions on the freedom of religion under Article 6 of the Constitution of the Kingdom of the Netherlands.

The Public Assemblies Act (Wet openbare manifestaties) regulates the exercise of and restrictions on the right of assembly and demonstration under Article 9 of the Constitution of the Kingdom of the Netherlands.

Under section 2 of the Public Assemblies Act, the power to restrict the rights of freedom of religion and assembly and demonstration as conferred on public authorities may be used only to protect health, in the interest of traffic and to combat or prevent disorder.
Under section 6 of the Public Assemblies Act, the Mayor may issue instructions which organisers of or participants in an assembly or demonstration must observe.

Under section 7 of the Public Assemblies Act, the Mayor may order the organisers or participants to end the assembly or demonstration forthwith and disperse if one of the interests referred to in section 2 of the Public Assemblies Act so requires.
Under section 11 of the Public Assemblies Act, the violation of the provisions of the Act is punishable by a term of detention not exceeding two months or a second-category fine.

The Amsterdam Court of Appeal held that the aim of the gathering on 5 July 2011 had been to seek confrontation with the Mobile Unit (Mobiele Eenheid) and to physically prevent the eviction of the Schijnheilig squat.

The Amsterdam Court of Appeal held that the gathering on 5 July 2011 could not be regarded as a demonstration in the sense of the Public Assemblies Act because its aim had been to seek confrontation with the Mobile Unit and to physically prevent the eviction.
The Amsterdam Court of Appeal held that public order had been disturbed within the meaning of section 2.2(1) of the Amsterdam general municipal by-law (APV) on 5 July 2011.

The Amsterdam Court of Appeal held that the facts on 5 July 2011 led to a disturbance of public order on the entire Passeerdersgracht within the meaning of section 2.2(1) of the Amsterdam general municipal by-law (APV).

The limited jurisdiction judge reasoned that according to section 2.2(4) of the Amsterdam general municipal by-law (APV), gatherings that have the character of a demonstration as referred to in the Public Assemblies Act (Wet openbare manifestaties) should be excluded from the scope of section 2.2 of the APV.

The limited jurisdiction judge was of the opinion that the gathering of the group of persons on 5 July 2011 was initially characterised more as a demonstration as referred to in the Public Assemblies Act than an unlawful gathering entailing disorder in the sense of section 2.2 of the Amsterdam general municipal by-law (APV).
The limited jurisdiction judge found that at the outset of the gathering on 5 July 2011 there was no threat of disorder.
The limited jurisdiction judge noted that a call had been made beforehand for all sympathisers of the Schijnheilig squat to make a statement against an empty city and in favour of free space.
The limited jurisdiction judge noted that the formal record of findings of the Police Commissioner indicated that the atmosphere was somewhat relaxed at the start of the gathering on 5 July 2011.

The limited jurisdiction judge noted that the group of persons at the gathering on 5 July 2011 stayed together almost continuously, sang along with musical instruments, chanted slogans, and performed dances together.

The limited jurisdiction judge noted that the public prosecutor stated at the hearing that four demonstrators wore wedding dresses and that their photos were taken by or with the cooperation of the police.
The limited jurisdiction judge concluded that at the outset of the gathering on 5 July 2011 there was a demonstration within the meaning of the Public Assemblies Act (Wet openbare manifestaties).
The limited jurisdiction judge found that it did not appear that the Mayor gave the police commissioner an order to end the demonstration on 5 July 2011.

The limited jurisdiction judge found that it was not possible to deduce from the documents and what was discussed at the hearing that the police order on 5 July 2011 was based on section 7 of the Public Assemblies Act.

The limited jurisdiction judge concluded that it was not established that the demonstration on 5 July 2011, which had originally been permitted and covered by the Public Assemblies Act, was at a later point in time no longer permitted under that Act.
The limited jurisdiction judge concluded that the demonstration on 5 July 2011 must be deemed to have remained permissible under the Public Assemblies Act.
The limited jurisdiction judge found that sections 2.2(1) and 2.2(3) of the Amsterdam general municipal by-law (APV) had been inapplicable pursuant to section 2.2(4) of the APV.
The applicants were acquitted by the limited jurisdiction judge of the offence of participating in an unlawful gathering or otherwise disturbing public order.
The applicants were discharged from prosecution by the limited jurisdiction judge for the offence of failing to comply with police orders to disperse.

The Amsterdam Court of Appeal considered that bringing air mattresses to the gathering served the purpose of protecting oneself against truncheons in the event of a confrontation with the Mobile Unit.

The Amsterdam Court of Appeal considered that wearing masks or balaclavas at the gathering served the purpose of protecting oneself against recognition in the event of a confrontation with the Mobile Unit.

The Amsterdam Court of Appeal noted that the Police Commissioner stated at the appeal hearing that it had been possible for persons from the group to leave the group but that it had been impossible for them to return to it afterwards.
The Amsterdam Court of Appeal noted that the persons in the group had plenty of time to leave the group before their arrest.
The Amsterdam Court of Appeal held that before the persons from the group were arrested there had been time and opportunity to leave the group that had been driven together.
The Amsterdam Court of Appeal held that the group of persons was not created by the action of the police, but the group stayed together voluntarily.
The Amsterdam Court of Appeal noted that the footage shows that at the moment of arrest, the group were sitting on the ground with their arms interlocked.

In their appeals on points of law to the Supreme Court, the applicants submitted that the protest had fallen within the scope of the Public Assemblies Act (Wet openbare manifestaties).

The Supreme Court held that the Amsterdam Court of Appeal had ruled not incomprehensibly that the aim of the gathering was to seek a confrontation with the Mobile Unit and to physically prevent the eviction.

The Supreme Court held that the Amsterdam Court of Appeal's ruling implied that the gathering did not primarily have the character of common expression of opinion, but was aimed at preventing the police from proceeding with the announced eviction by means of de facto coercion.

The Supreme Court held that the Amsterdam Court of Appeal did not err in law and was not incomprehensible in ruling that there was no question of a demonstration within the meaning of the Public Assemblies Act and that the conduct of those present fell within the scope of section 2.2 of the Amsterdam general municipal by-law (APV).

The Supreme Court held that the applicants' argument concerning a broad interpretation of the right to freedom of assembly as protected by Article 11 of the Convention did not necessitate a different conclusion.
